questions.q: Which access pattern does object storage natively support?
options: Whole-object reads and writes over HTTP, addressed by key
In-place overwrite of arbitrary byte ranges in the middle of stored data
POSIX file locking shared safely across many clients
Mounting as a raw block device with fsync semantics
questions.explanation: Object stores expose a flat key-to-blob namespace over a REST API. Objects are immutable units, so there is no in-place editing, no locking, and no filesystem semantics.

questions.q: What does a presigned URL grant in S3-style storage?
options: Permanent public read access to the whole bucket
Time-limited access to one object, using the signer's permissions
Anonymous listing of every bucket in the account
A way to bypass bucket policies for as long as the link is shared
questions.explanation: The signature embeds the key, HTTP method, and an expiry, and it can never exceed the signing principal's own permissions. It is delegated, narrowly scoped access.

questions.q: Why use multipart upload for a large object?
options: It compresses each part automatically before transfer
It encrypts every part with a separate key for stronger security
Parts upload in parallel and a failed part can be retried alone
It splits the object into many small objects to dodge size limits
questions.explanation: Multipart gives throughput through parallelism and resilience through granular retries, so a network blip costs one part instead of the entire transfer. The result is still one object.

questions.q: Since 2020, what consistency does Amazon S3 provide?
options: Eventual consistency for overwrite PUTs only
Strong consistency only for requests within one availability zone
Eventual consistency for LIST operations after a recent PUT
Strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs, including LISTs
questions.explanation: S3 became strongly consistent in December 2020: a successful write is immediately visible to subsequent GETs and LISTs, eliminating the old read-after-overwrite workarounds.

questions.q: What is the core tradeoff of archive storage classes like Glacier?
options: Much cheaper storage in exchange for slow, costlier retrieval
Higher durability than the standard class at the same price
Faster reads because data is compacted onto dense media
Free retrievals in exchange for a long minimum storage commitment
questions.explanation: Archive tiers cut per-GB storage cost by an order of magnitude but add restore delays from minutes to hours plus per-GB retrieval fees, so they only pay off for rarely read data.

questions.q: Which workload is a better fit for block storage than object storage?
options: Serving a static website's images to browsers
Storing nightly database backup archives
A relational database's live data files needing random writes
Retaining several months of application log archives
questions.explanation: A live database needs low-latency random reads and writes to arbitrary offsets, which only block devices provide. The other three are write-once, read-whole workloads.

questions.q: S3's famous 'eleven nines' figure describes what?
options: Availability of GET requests over a year
Durability — the probability an object is not lost
The latency SLA at the 99.999999999th percentile of requests
Uptime of the bucket's regional endpoints
questions.explanation: Durability is about not losing data and comes from redundancy across devices and zones. Availability, whether you can reach it right now, is a much lower number like 99.99%.

questions.q: How is an existing object modified in object storage?
options: Appends rewrite only the final block
Byte edits are patched in place on disk
The service applies delta encoding to store only the changes by default
The whole object is rewritten, or a new version is created
questions.explanation: Objects are immutable, so any change means uploading a complete replacement under the same key; with versioning enabled that replacement becomes a new version.

questions.q: A single PUT of a 500 GB file to S3 fails immediately. Why?
options: A single PUT caps at 5 GB; multipart upload is required
S3 limits every object to 100 GB regardless of method
Presigned URLs are mandatory for uploads of this size
The bucket must have versioning enabled before accepting large uploads
questions.explanation: The 5 GB ceiling applies to one PUT, not to objects: multipart upload raises the maximum object size to 5 TB by assembling many parts server-side.

questions.q: A presigned PUT URL leaks publicly. What limits the damage?
options: S3 detects the anomalous traffic and quarantines the link automatically
It expires and is scoped to one method and one object key
It only works from the original requester's IP address
The attacker would also need the bucket's access policy
questions.explanation: The signature covers the method, key, and expiry, so a leaked link only lets someone overwrite that one object until it expires. Short expiries keep the window small.

questions.q: Uploads often crash mid-way. No new objects appear, yet the storage bill keeps climbing. Likely cause?
options: Versioning is silently retaining old copies of the failed files
Abandoned multipart parts persist until aborted; add a lifecycle rule
The bucket charges per initiated request, not per byte
Failed uploads are retried server-side and stored in a hidden tier
questions.explanation: Uploaded parts are billed storage even though the object never completes and never appears in LIST. An AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule reclaims them automatically.

questions.q: One key prefix returns '503 Slow Down' at high request rates. Best fix?
options: Spread keys across more prefixes to raise the request-rate ceiling
Enable versioning so the request load distributes across object versions
Move the data to an infrequent-access storage class
Batch objects together so each request moves more bytes
questions.explanation: S3 scales request capacity per key prefix as it partitions the index, so hashing or randomizing the leading path segment spreads load across partitions.

questions.q: Data is read roughly once per quarter but needs millisecond access when requested. Best storage class?
options: Glacier Deep Archive, for the lowest possible cost
Standard, since retrieval fees never matter at this request volume
Standard-Infrequent Access: cheaper storage, instant reads, retrieval fee
One Zone-IA, because quarterly data needs less durability
questions.explanation: Standard-IA keeps the same millisecond latency and multi-AZ durability at lower per-GB cost, and the retrieval fee is negligible at quarterly reads. Glacier's restore delay violates the latency need.

questions.q: App servers saturate their bandwidth proxying large downloads from object storage. Standard fix?
options: Add more app servers to spread the proxy load
Cache the hottest files on every app server's local SSD ahead of demand
Compress all objects at rest to shrink transfer sizes
Hand clients presigned GET URLs so they download directly
questions.explanation: Presigned URLs keep authorization in the app while moving the bytes out of it, so the object store or CDN serves the payload and app bandwidth stops being the bottleneck.

questions.q: After enabling versioning, deleting objects no longer reduces the bill. Why?
options: Deletes just add a delete marker; versions persist until lifecycle rules expire them
Versioned buckets never physically remove any data, ever
Delete requests are asynchronous and can lag behind by several weeks
Billing meters update only when the bucket is fully emptied
questions.explanation: In a versioned bucket a plain DELETE is non-destructive: it hides the object behind a marker while all prior versions remain billable until explicitly deleted or expired.

questions.q: You compare a downloaded file's MD5 against the object's ETag; big files always mismatch. Why?
options: Server-side encryption changes the stored bytes and therefore their hash
Multipart ETags hash the part hashes, not the whole file
ETags are random identifiers regenerated on every read
MD5 is unreliable above the 4 GB boundary on most platforms
questions.explanation: A multipart ETag is the MD5 of the concatenated part MD5s with a -N part-count suffix, so it can never equal the whole-file MD5. Use checksum headers instead.

questions.q: Two clients PUT the same key at the same moment in an unversioned bucket. What is guaranteed?
options: The second writer receives a conflict error and must retry the upload
The two payloads are merged byte-wise in arrival order
Last writer wins; there is no locking or conflict detection
Both are kept and exposed as sibling versions
questions.explanation: Object stores offer no compare-and-swap by default, so concurrent PUTs simply race and one silently overwrites the other. Versioning or conditional writes are needed to detect it.

questions.q: Objects in Standard-IA are each read about ten times a month, and the bill now exceeds Standard. Why?
options: IA's higher request latency triggers client retries that multiply request charges
A minimum object size surcharge applies to every read
IA replicates to fewer zones, adding a risk premium fee
Per-GB retrieval fees at that read rate outweigh the storage discount
questions.explanation: IA trades a lower storage rate for a per-GB retrieval charge. Read the data often enough and the retrieval charges accumulate past the storage savings, inverting the economics.

questions.q: Why do object stores favor erasure coding over 3x replication for cold data?
options: It makes small random reads faster by spreading load across many disks
It removes the need for periodic checksum scrubbing entirely
Comparable durability at roughly 1.5x storage overhead instead of 3x
It allows partial in-place updates of stored stripes
questions.explanation: Splitting data into k fragments plus m parity fragments tolerates m losses while storing far less than three full copies. The cost is CPU for encoding and slower reconstruction reads.

questions.q: A pipeline 'renames' millions of objects daily and is slow and surprisingly expensive. Why?
options: Each rename rebalances the storage cluster's hash ring
Renames force synchronous CDN invalidations that block until every edge confirms
Renamed objects must be re-uploaded from the client side
There is no rename; each one is a server-side copy plus delete
questions.explanation: The flat keyspace has no rename primitive, so every move rewrites the full object bytes under the new key and then deletes the old one, costing time and request charges.
